title: Early Credit-Card Fraud Detection via Behavior-Deviation Sequence Modeling
content: Credit-card fraud detection protects the payment networks through which issuers, merchants, and cardholders transact, and it must decide under a fixed alert budget which transactions to stop. Sequence models capture cardholder behavior more faithfully than models that score each transaction in isolation, but most prior works evaluated them with aggregate metrics that treat every fraudulent transaction of a compromised card as equally valuable, hiding how early in a fraud burst the detector fires, which is what determines the realized loss. We propose DevSeq, a behavior-deviation sequence model for early card-fraud detection that explicitly represents how far a transaction departs from the cardholder's own habits. DevSeq first encodes the recent transaction sequence of a card with a Transformer encoder and summarizes the long-term habits of the same card with a causal behavioral profile, then derives an explicit deviation representation by cross-attending the current transaction to the recent sequence and by comparing it against the projected long-term profile, and finally adds a self-supervised next-transaction prediction task that requires no fraud labels. We further propose a burst-level evaluation protocol that, under a fixed alert budget, separates the first fraudulent transaction of a fraud burst from the subsequent ones and reports the loss incurred before the first alert. On a public synthetic dataset of 24 million card transactions under a temporal split, DevSeq raises first-transaction recall at a 0.5% alert budget from 0.182 for an aggregation-feature baseline and 0.268 for the strongest sequence baseline to 0.342, and reduces the mean loss before the first alert from 199.1 to 152.8 USD. With only 10% of the fraud labels, DevSeq still exceeds the aggregation baseline trained with all of them.
